description: The hand-verified expected result for the negative Opengrep SARIF fixture that carries one record from which no rule identifier can be obtained by either route. Every value was derived by reading the fixture and the authored contracts in harness/lib/normalize/, never by running the adapter and recording what it printed. Where this file and harness/lib/normalize/adapters/sarif.py disagree, the disagreement is the finding: diagnose it rather than overwriting this file to match. The key names are the ones expected/reject-sarif-unresolvable-path.rows.json established as the template every negative expected file in this folder follows -- routing, rejection_boundary, rows, row_derivations, rejections, counts, counters and counts.parse_status all carry the same meanings here -- with one additive block, rule_identifier_resolution, because the two-route identifier lookup is the whole subject of this fixture and no other expected file records it.

fixture.derivation: A negative fixture is derived from the captured artifact rather than being an excerpt of it, so the provenance is stated as a derivation, record by record. /runs/0/results/0 is unmodified captured output: byte-identical to harness/artifacts/raw/opengrep.sarif results[432] and to the positive fixture's results[1]. /runs/0/results/1 is the defective record: it is that artifact's results[521] -- the captured avoid-pickle finding on python/pyspark/ml/tests/connect/test_legacy_mode_feature.py:90, which the positive fixture also carries as its results[2] -- with exactly one change, its ruleId removed and a ruleIndex of 99 put in its place; its fingerprints, locations, message and properties are carried over untouched. /runs/0/results/2 is the synthesized companion: a hardcoded-conditional finding on common/network-shuffle/src/main/java/org/apache/spark/network/shuffle/OneForOneBlockPusher.java:159 whose identifier is expressed only as a ruleIndex of 0, so the fixture proves the index route works when the index is in range as well as proving what happens when it is not. The driver rules array is trimmed to the three rules these records need, which is exactly what makes 99 out of range and index 0 land on hardcoded-conditional.
fixture.captured_provenance: Checked rather than asserted. /runs/0/results/0 compared equal to raw results[432] as whole objects. /runs/0/results/1 compared equal to raw results[521] under the single substitution described above -- the only key that differs is the identifier. /runs/0/results/2 appears in no captured artifact: the sole hardcoded-conditional record in harness/artifacts/raw/opengrep.sarif names common/network-common/src/main/java/org/apache/spark/network/buffer/FileSegmentManagedBuffer.java:112, harness/artifacts/raw/semgrep.sarif carries no OneForOneBlockPusher record at all, and the single one in harness/artifacts/raw/datadog-static-analyzer.sarif is at line 68 under a different rule; it also lacks the fingerprints object every captured Opengrep result carries. Its content is real rather than invented even so: the snippet is verbatim lines 159 to 162 of the pinned OneForOneBlockPusher.java, and the message is /runs/0/tool/driver/rules/0/fullDescription/text verbatim. The recorded sha256 above is what makes a later edit to the fixture visible: these values are re-derived when the fixture changes, never adjusted to keep a test green.
fixture.recorded_rule_pointers_note: Three rules are declared and only two are used by a surviving row. /runs/0/tool/driver/rules/1 is the avoid-pickle rule the defective record would have resolved to had it stated its ruleId, and it is deliberately left in place: the rule the record belongs to being present and reachable by id is what rules out "the rule is simply not declared" as an alternative explanation for the rejection. The record cannot reach it, because a ruleIndex of 99 names no element of a three-element array and nothing else on the record names the rule.
fixture.not_records: The two entries under /runs/0/invocations/0/toolExecutionNotifications are tool notifications -- one rule timeout and one syntax error over vendored minified JavaScript -- and are not finding records. They are neither rows nor rejections and are not counted: a reading that counted anything finding-shaped would arrive at five records and fail the reconciliation identity for a reason that has nothing to do with the adapter.

routing.detected_by: normalize.shape.is_sarif -- a version of "2.1.0" together with a runs array; those two together are the whole test
routing.routing_decision: normalize.shape.route("opengrep", doc) returns tool "opengrep", shape "sarif", adapter "sarif", scanner_class "sast"
routing.not_a_shape_failure: No normalize.shape.UnknownArtifactShape is expected here, and a test asserting one against this fixture would be asserting the wrong thing. The enclosing document is valid SARIF 2.1.0 and routes cleanly; exactly one record inside it is defective, and the adapter rejects that record while still emitting the others. The fixtures that own shape-detection failure are near-sarif-version-only.json, near-sarif-runs-only.json and unknown-shape.json.
routing.negative_routing_test: The mandated negative routing assertion -- that a native artifact must not route to the SARIF adapter -- belongs to test_shape_routing_negative.py and does not use this fixture.

rule_identifier_resolution.why_this_fixture_exists: To assert the one rejection condition that cannot be produced by removing a field. Every other SARIF rejection condition has a single source -- one path, one message, one start_line -- so deleting or corrupting that source produces the rejection. A rule identifier has more than one source, and AAP 0.5.4 requires every one of them tried before the record is rejected: rule_id comes from ruleId, "resolved through runs[].tool.driver.rules[] by ruleIndex where absent". A record that merely lacks ruleId is therefore a well-formed record that the adapter must still emit, and only a record that defeats every route has no identifier at all.

routes_the_adapter_implements.source: the id of the rule at the result's ruleIndex, in the rules array of the toolComponent that index is scoped to -- tool.driver where no toolComponent is referenced, which is SARIF's own default
routes_the_adapter_implements.present_in_this_fixture: attempted on /runs/0/results/1 with an index of 99, and successful on /runs/0/results/2 with an index of 0

routes_the_adapter_implements.source: a rule reporting-descriptor reference on the result -- its id, or its index scoped to its toolComponent
routes_the_adapter_implements.present_in_this_fixture: on no result; no record here carries a rule reference, so the two routes actually in play are ruleId and ruleIndex

rule_identifier_resolution.both_routes_must_be_tried: The adapter's _resolve_rule reads ruleId first and, where no identifier was established that way, applies the index. Only when both have been tried and neither yielded a non-empty string is rule_id None, which is the missing_rule_id condition. This file asserts that ordering twice over: once as a rejection, on the record that defeats both, and once as a row, on the record that succeeds through the index alone.
rule_identifier_resolution.deleting_rule_id_is_not_enough: A fixture whose defective record simply omitted ruleId would assert nothing about this condition, because the index route would still resolve the identifier and the correct outcome would be a row. Worse, such a fixture would be *satisfied* by an implementation that rejects any result lacking ruleId -- exactly the defect this fixture is built to catch -- so the assertion would pass while the implementation silently discarded good findings from every index-using producer.
rule_identifier_resolution.how_this_fixture_defeats_both_routes: /runs/0/results/1 carries no ruleId key at all -- its keys are exactly fingerprints, locations, message, properties and ruleIndex -- and no rule reference, so route 1 and route 3 have nothing to read. Its ruleIndex of 99 is out of range for the three rules on tool.driver, so route 2 reaches no rule object and therefore no id. Both routes are exhausted by construction rather than by luck.
rule_identifier_resolution.out_of_range_index_must_be_bounds_checke: An out-of-range index is artifact content, so it must become a reason rather than an exception. harness/lib/normalize/adapters/sarif.py's _RuleTable.rule_by_index tests 0 <= index < len(component.rules) and returns (None, reason) -- and returns a distinct reason for a non-integer index and for an array element that is not an object -- so no route through it can raise IndexError. The caller turns that reason into the rejection's detail.
rule_identifier_resolution.why_an_uncaught_index_error_would_be_wor: It would abandon the artifact mid-walk. Every record after the defective one would be lost, the emitted-row count would silently depend on where in the file the defect happened to sit, and the reconciliation identity raw finding records = dataset rows + rejected records could not balance for any tool sharing this adapter -- so the failure would surface as an arithmetic mismatch a reader would have to trace back to a crash. Rejecting the one record and carrying on keeps both the loss and its reason visible and countable. This fixture proves the carry-on directly: the defective record is the middle of three, and the third record's row is expected precisely so that a crash cannot pass as a pass.
rule_identifier_resolution.no_synthesised_identifier: The rejected record is rejected and counted, never given an identifier. Nothing in this file supplies one for it -- not the rule name of the rule it plainly belongs to, not a slug from its message, not its path, not the index literal 99, and not a placeholder such as "unknown". AAP 0.5.4's reject-rather-than-infer applies to the identifier exactly as it applies to a path.
rule_identifier_resolution.rule_metadata_is_lost_with_the_identifie: Because no rule object is reached, no severity, CWE or CVE could have been read from the rule even if the record had been emitted. That is recorded as a consequence of the same failure and not as a second condition: rule_metadata_unresolved counts it once, and no severity or path counter moves for this record at all.

field_order_authority: harness/lib/normalize/emit.py, the FIELDS constant. Every row below carries all twelve keys in that order, present-with-null rather than omitted.
absence_convention: Absence is JSON null here and in findings.json, and an empty field in findings.csv. tool, scanner_class, rule_id, message, severity_norm, path and in_scope are never absent -- exactly emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS.

allowlist.note: in_scope is decided by that file alone. The globs are not copied here: the allowlist is the single authority and stays byte-exact. The glob each row matched is recorded per row under row_derivations.

resolution_context.root_independence: Both surviving uris are already root-relative, and the recorded path base for opengrep is the scan root itself, so joining onto the base and relativizing back to the root returns each uri unchanged. These rows therefore hold for whatever absolute scan root the adapter is given, and no absolute path appears anywhere in this file. The rejected record is root-independent for a different reason from the unresolvable-path fixture's: its path is a perfectly ordinary root-relative uri that would have resolved under any root, and it is rejected before the resolver is ever consulted.
resolution_context.path_base_source: harness/artifacts/logs/runner-metadata.json, the opengrep entry's path_base -- read as input, never assumed
resolution_context.uri_base_id_walk_consequence: With no run.originalUriBaseIds the SARIF 2.1.0 section 3.4.4 procedure cannot complete -- the documented producer gap -- and that outcome is eligible for the metadata-backed fallback, so each surviving path resolves against the runner-recorded base rather than being rejected. The defective record never reaches this walk either, but for a different reason than in the unresolvable-path fixture: there the foreign scheme was classified inside the resolver, here the record is rejected two steps earlier and the resolver is never called.
resolution_context.severity_source: Neither surviving result states a level, and neither of their rules carries properties.severity or properties.problem.severity, so each severity_native is the level its own rule states under defaultConfiguration.level and each severity_norm comes from the SARIF level table: error High, warning Medium, note Low, none Info. Both rules in play state error, so both rows are High.
resolution_context.package_coordinate: null on every row. A SARIF result names a code location rather than a package, and this shape supplies no coordinate to carry.

rejection_boundary.statement: A record from which no rule identifier can be obtained by any route is a rejection. A record whose identifier is merely awkward to obtain -- stated only as an index, or naming a rule the artifact does not declare -- is a kept row. This fixture's defective record can reach no identifier at all, which is what makes it the missing_rule_id case rather than one of the kept cases below.
rejection_boundary.why_it_can_only_be_a_rejection: rule_id is one of emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS: emit.OPTIONAL_FIELDS is exactly severity_native, start_line, cwe, cve and package_coordinate, and AAP 0.8.2 permits absence on those five and no others. A record with no obtainable identifier therefore has no valid row representation at all -- emit.py raises on a null required field rather than writing one -- so counting it under a named class is the only outcome that neither drops the record nor invents an identifier for it.

not_a_rejection.case: an identifier stated only as a ruleIndex, with no ruleId
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row whose rule_id is the indexed rule's id, counted under rule_id_from_rule_index
not_a_rejection.evidence: This is the case a naive implementation gets wrong, so it is the one case this fixture demonstrates rather than merely describes: /runs/0/results/2 is exactly it, and its row is required below.

not_a_rejection.case: an identifier that resolves to no rule object -- a producer emitting ruleId with no rules array, or naming a rule the array does not declare
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row; the identifier is known and only the metadata is missing, so severity_native, cwe and cve simply have no source and take their absent values
not_a_rejection.evidence: The adapter's _RuleResolution keeps rule_id and rule independent for exactly this reason: rule is None where the identifier is known but the rule object is not, and only rule_id being None is the rejection condition.

not_a_rejection.case: a usable ruleId alongside an unusable ruleIndex
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row, with rule_index_unusable counting the failed index and rule_id_from_rule_id counting the identifier that succeeded
not_a_rejection.evidence: rule_index_unusable is a provenance counter, not a rejection counter; the two coincide in this fixture only because its one unusable index sits on a record with no other identifier.

rejection_boundary.defective_record_reaches_no_identifier: Verified from the fixture rather than assumed. /runs/0/results/1 has exactly the keys fingerprints, locations, message, properties and ruleIndex: there is no ruleId to read and no rule reference to read an id or a scoped index from. Its ruleIndex is 99 and /runs/0/tool/driver/rules holds three elements, so the index names no element, no rule object is returned, and no id can be taken from one. Both available routes are exhausted, and no third reading of the record exists.
rejection_boundary.attribution_is_to_the_identifier_alone: Asserted, not assumed, because the assertion this file carries is on the rejection *class* and a record defective in two ways could be counted under either class while a test that only counts rejections still passed. Every other property of /runs/0/results/1 was hand-checked against the fixture and the pinned tree and is well-formed: the results element is a JSON object, so step 1 would pass; message.text is present and non-empty, so step 3 would pass; locations[0].physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri is python/pyspark/ml/tests/connect/test_legacy_mode_feature.py, an ordinary root-relative path naming a file that exists in the pinned tree and falls inside the glob python/pyspark/**, so step 4 would pass; and region.startLine is the integer 90, which is within that file and is the line the record's own snippet quotes -- `sk_model = pickle.load(f)` -- so step 5 would pass. Step 2 is the only step that fails, and missing_rule_id is therefore the only class the record can be counted under.
rejection_boundary.later_steps_are_never_examined: The rejection is raised at step 2, so the adapter never reads this record's message, path or start_line, and none of their would-be values appears in any row in this file. The previous key establishes that those fields are sound; this key establishes that soundness is a property of the fixture rather than something the adapter checks here. Both are worth stating: the first is why the class is attributable, the second is why no path, severity or start_line counter moves for this record.
rejection_boundary.no_guessed_identifier_and_no_guessed_row: The rejected record contributes no row, no identifier and no field of any kind. Nothing in this file supplies a plausible substitute for what it could not resolve.

counts.raw_count_unit: one element of runs[].results[] -- the unit normalize.reconcile.count_records walks independently of row construction
counts.raw_count_authority: normalize.reconcile.count_records("opengrep", doc), whose SARIF traversal sums the length of each run's results array and builds no row, resolves no rule, resolves no path and maps no severity. It is the independent half of the identity: a count taken from the traversal that builds the rows would satisfy the assertion while testing nothing.

four_reported_counters.authority: AAP 0.5.4 -- the four counts reported per tool
four_reported_counters.note: Named here rather than restated with their values. The counters block below is the single measurement, and a number carried twice inside one document is a number that can drift; counters_note gives the reason each of the four is zero.

counts.parse_status_authority: harness/lib/normalize/cli.py, PARSE_STATUS_PARTIAL = "partial", assigned as partial where there are rejections and clean where there are none. Partial is right precisely because the adapter did not abandon the artifact: every parsable record was emitted and the one rejected record is counted under its class, with its reason retained. This is deliberately not normalize.reconcile's STATUS_PASS / STATUS_FAIL / STATUS_NOT_APPLICABLE vocabulary, which describes an assertion's outcome rather than an artifact's parse.

counters_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/sarif.py, COUNTER_KEYS as returned by new_counters(): twenty authored keys, one path_kind_* per normalize.paths.PATH_KINDS member and one severity_basis_* per normalize.severity.BASIS_VALUES member, twenty-nine in total.
counters_note: Four things a reader must not "correct", all of them the classification order made visible. First, rule_id_from_rule_id and rule_id_from_rule_index sum to 2 rather than 3: those two counters record where a *resolved* identifier came from, and the rejected record resolved none, so it increments neither. That is the opposite of the unresolvable-path fixture, where the rejected record resolved its identifier at step 2 and was rejected at step 4, leaving rule_id_from_rule_id at 3 over two rows -- the same order producing the mirror-image asymmetry. Second, rule_index_unusable is 1 and rule_metadata_unresolved is 1, and both are the same record counted once each for two different facts: its index could not be applied, and with neither an id nor an indexed object no rule metadata could be reached. Neither counter equals the rejection count in general, and a fixture where they diverge is described under rejection_boundary.not_a_rejection. Third, the severity and path counters total 2, not 3, because the rejected record never reaches steps 4 and 5. Fourth, the four counters AAP 0.5.4 has reported per tool are all 0 here: every result carries exactly one location, so multi_location_records is 0; the one rule behind an emitted row that names a weakness names exactly one, so multi_valued_cwe_records is 0; no rule string carries a CVE identifier, so multi_valued_cve_records is 0; and both emitted paths name a file inside the scanned tree, so non_filesystem_paths is 0.

corroboration.note: Only row 0 has a counterpart to corroborate against: it is the same captured result the positive sibling covers, and all twelve field comparisons agree. Recorded after the fact rather than as the source of these values -- each value here was derived from the fixture and the authored contracts, so a future disagreement between this file and the adapter is a finding to diagnose rather than a diff to apply. Row 1 has no counterpart because it is this fixture's own synthesized companion, and the rejected record has none for the same reason and contributes no dataset row either way. The raw count needs no corroboration: /runs/0/results holds three elements and there is one run, so the count unit's arithmetic is visible in the fixture itself.

rows.message: User data flows into this manually-constructed SQL string. User data can be safely inserted into SQL strings using prepared statements or an object-relational mapper (ORM). Manually-constructed SQL strings is a possible indicator of SQL injection, which could let an attacker steal or manipulate data from the database. Instead, use prepared statements (`connection.PreparedStatement`) or a safe library.
This if statement will always have the same behavior and is therefore unnecessary.

row_derivations.rule_id_source: the result's own ruleId; no ruleIndex and no rule reference is present
row_derivations.severity_native_note: the result states no level, and its rule carries neither properties.severity nor properties.problem.severity, so all three field sources AAP 0.5.4 authorises for a SARIF record are silent; the absence is stated rather than filled from rule.defaultConfiguration.level, which AAP 0.5.4 does not carry as a field source

cwe_source.text: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

row_derivations.anchor_note: The record that precedes the defective one, so a rejection cannot pass as a pass by emitting nothing at all. Line 72 of the pinned DiskStore.scala is the interpolated string argument of the SparkException.internalError(...) call that opens on line 71, and the file is 380 lines, so start_line is within the file. This row's rule identifier travels the direct route, which is what makes the pair with row 1 a route-by-route assertion rather than a single case repeated.

row_derivations.rule_id_source: no ruleId is present on the result; the identifier is the id at /runs/0/tool/driver/rules/0, reached through the result's ruleIndex of 0

rule_index.component_source: the result carries no rule.toolComponent reference, and an absent reference means the driver -- SARIF's own default

row_derivations.severity_native_note: the result states no level, and its rule carries neither properties.severity nor properties.problem.severity, so all three field sources AAP 0.5.4 authorises for a SARIF record are silent; the absence is stated rather than filled from rule.defaultConfiguration.level, which AAP 0.5.4 does not carry as a field source
row_derivations.cwe_absent_reason: the rule carries no properties.cwe and its properties.tags array is empty, so no CWE token exists to collect
row_derivations.must_be_present: This row is not optional and its absence is a failure rather than a shortfall. Without it the fixture is satisfied by an implementation that rejects any result lacking ruleId: that implementation would produce one rejection and one row here, the rejection count would match, and the assertion would pass -- while in production it would silently discard every finding from a producer that states its identifier as an index. The row is the only thing in this file that distinguishes "tried both routes and neither worked" from "only ever tried the first route".
row_derivations.anchor_note: A different module and a different rule from row 0, so the fixture also proves the adapter carried on past the rejection rather than merely emitting the record that preceded it. start_line 159 is the `if (blockIdParts.length != 5 || ...)` statement whose block closes at 162 -- the four lines the record's own snippet quotes verbatim -- and the pinned file is 171 lines, so start_line is within the file.

rejections.locator_note: The pointer and the run_index / result_index pair name the same record. The pair is carried as well because normalize.adapters.sarif passes exactly run_index and result_index into the rejection it builds for this condition, so a produced Rejection's record_identity and this expectation can be compared directly, without translating one coordinate system into the other.
rejections.reject_class_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, the REJECT_MISSING_RULE_ID constant -- a literal member of paths.REJECT_CLASSES, the closed set of ten. Written verbatim rather than paraphrased, and asserted against the module rather than by eye: a test that only counts rejections cannot tell one condition from another, so the class name is what carries the assertion.
rejections.classification_step: step 2 of the adapter's fixed classification order -- shape, rule identifier, message, path, start_line. Step 1 passes: the results element is a JSON object. Step 2 is where it fails, and steps 3, 4 and 5 are never reached.

rule_id_routes_attempted.outcome: no ruleId key is present; the record's keys are exactly fingerprints, locations, message, properties and ruleIndex

rule_id_routes_attempted.route: id on a rule reporting-descriptor reference
rule_id_routes_attempted.outcome: no rule reference is present, so there is no id to read

rule_id_routes_attempted.route: the id of the rule at ruleIndex, in the referenced component's rules array
rule_id_routes_attempted.outcome: the index is out of range, so no rule object is returned and no id can be taken from one

rule_index.component_source: the result carries no rule.toolComponent reference, and an absent reference means the driver, so the component resolves cleanly and tool_component_reference_unresolved stays 0
rule_index.bounds_check_outcome: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/sarif.py's _RuleTable.rule_by_index tests 0 <= index < len(component.rules) and returns no rule together with a reason naming the range it fell outside. It does not raise: an out-of-range index is artifact content, and AAP 0.5.4 requires it handled as data.
rule_index.must_not_raise: An uncaught IndexError here would abandon the artifact at this record, losing every later record -- including row 1 below -- and leaving the reconciliation identity unbalanceable. The fixture places the defective record between two sound ones precisely so that a crash cannot be mistaken for a correct rejection.
rule_index.other_unusable_index_reasons_not_exercis: rule_by_index distinguishes three further reasons -- a non-integer index, an index whose component could not be resolved, and a rules array element that is not an object -- each of which also yields a reason rather than an exception. This fixture exercises only the out-of-range reason.

rejections.expected_detail: the result carries no usable ruleId, and no rule could be reached through ruleIndex either: ruleIndex 99 is out of range for the 3 rules on tool.driver
rejections.expected_detail_note: The detail is the sub-reason AAP 0.5.4 requires a rejection to carry, and it is quoted here because this class covers several routes: naming the class alone would not distinguish this record from one whose index was a string, or whose toolComponent could not be resolved. A test may assert the class exactly and the detail by its distinguishing substrings -- "no usable ruleId", "99", "out of range", "3 rules", "tool.driver" -- rather than by full-string equality, since the prose composes the adapter's own two messages.
rejections.record_identity_note: Two keys rather than the unresolvable-path fixture's five, and the difference is the point rather than an omission. No rule_id is carried because there is none to carry -- carrying the string the record plainly belongs to would be the synthesis this condition exists to forbid -- and no uri or uriBaseId is carried because the path step is never reached, so the resolver that adds them is never called. The pair is still enough to find the record in the artifact again, and it is never the record itself and never a secret value.
rejections.why_not_a_row: There is no identifier to put in the row. rule_id is never absent from a row, so a record whose identifier cannot be obtained by any route has no valid row representation, and the alternatives -- dropping it, or giving it an identifier taken from its message, its path, its rule's name or the index literal -- would each hide it or misattribute it. Counting it under a named class keeps it visible and keeps the arithmetic honest.
rejections.contributes_no_severity_literal: The rejected record is never fed to the severity tally, so no native literal from it reaches severity-map.md. That document reports literals against the rows the dataset contains, and this record contributes none. Its rule's level of warning appears nowhere in this file for the same reason -- the rule was never reached.
rejections.contributes_no_path_or_scope_counter: path_kind_tree_file is 2 rather than 3 and rows_in_scope is 2 rather than 3, even though this record's path is an ordinary in-scope file. Steps 4 and 5 are never reached, so neither the path kind nor the in_scope decomposition sees it -- and no row means no in_scope value at all, not in_scope false.
rejections.not_produced_by_a_path_condition: The five reject-sarif-uribaseid-* fixtures own the base-resolution terminal cases and reject-sarif-unresolvable-path.sarif owns the coordinate that resolves to nothing. This record's path is sound and is never examined, so this fixture re-covers none of what those six cover and each of them still has its own work to do.

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: shape-detection failure -- an artifact matching neither SARIF nor a known native shape halting the run
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: this document is valid SARIF 2.1.0 and routes cleanly; its defect is one record, not its shape

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: the six other rejection conditions this adapter can reach -- absent_path, unresolvable_path, invalid_uri, missing_message, non_integer_start_line and malformed_record; seven with missing_rule_id, which is the full set the SARIF path can produce
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: this fixture isolates one condition, so exactly one record is defective and it is defective in exactly one way
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.cover_with: the sibling negative fixtures in this tree -- reject-sarif-unresolvable-path.sarif, reject-sarif-malformed-record.sarif, reject-sarif-missing-message.sarif, reject-sarif-non-integer-start-line.sarif and the five reject-sarif-uribaseid-* fixtures. Which condition each of those asserts is stated in its own expected file, not here.

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: the three unusable-index reasons other than out-of-range -- a non-integer ruleIndex, an index whose toolComponent reference could not be resolved, and a rules array element that is not an object
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.why_absent: one defective record can only fail one way, and out-of-range is the reason this fixture fixes; all four reasons converge on the same rejection class, so the class assertion here holds for each of them
behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.cover_with: derived fixtures carrying a string ruleIndex, a rule.toolComponent reference that resolves to nothing, and a rules array whose indexed element is not an object

behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture.behaviour: rule metadata reached through an extension toolComponent, and a known identifier whose rule object cannot be found at all
